clue.text: Message on X, dry with little in it (5)

indicators.note: the little word is placed inside the dry one

annotation.surface: Someone describes a short, dry post on social media.
annotation.walkthrough: X is the platform formerly called Twitter, where posts were named after birdsong. 'Dry' here means not drinking alcohol, a sense a solver may not reach for first.
annotation.definitionFit: A tweet was the name for a message posted on Twitter, now X.

clue.text: Eric Cantona’s moving around, crossing the Atlantic perhaps (12)

indicators.note: the letters are shifted about into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters, including the S of the possessive

annotation.surface: The French footballer Eric Cantona is on the move, perhaps heading across the Atlantic.
annotation.walkthrough: Eric Cantona was a French footballer famous at Manchester United; the possessive S is part of the fodder. 'Perhaps' flags the Atlantic as just one example of an ocean.
annotation.definitionFit: Transoceanic means crossing an ocean, and the Atlantic is one such ocean.

clue.text: Imposing new fencing to protect gold (9)

indicators.note: the letters of 'fencing' are made new, i.e. rearranged
the rearranged letters surround and guard the gold

annotation.surface: Someone installs new, impressive fencing to keep gold safe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Imposing' reads as an adjective (grand) but is the verb form: enforcing a rule is imposing it. ENF(OR)CING.
annotation.definitionFit: To enforce a rule is to impose it, so enforcing means imposing.

clue.text: Unexpected plot development for Dickens hero (5)

blocks.note: a sudden turn in a story's plot
surname of Oliver, the orphan hero of a Dickens novel

annotation.surface: A writer plans a surprise turn in the story for a Dickens hero.
annotation.walkthrough: Oliver Twist is the orphan hero of Charles Dickens's novel of that name.
annotation.definitionFit: A twist is an unexpected turn in a plot; Twist is also Oliver's surname.

clue.text: Peculiar pathogen’s shape (8)

indicators.note: the letters are made odd, i.e. rearranged

annotation.surface: A scientist remarks on the odd form of a germ under the microscope.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s is read as 'has', linking the wordplay to the definition: the rearranged pathogen has the shape.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by category: this seven-sided figure is one kind of shape.

clue.text: He had, for example, upset greedy people and prickly sorts (9)

indicators.note: in a down clue, set upside down turns the letters bottom to top

blocks.note: he had = he'd, without the apostrophe
EG = for example, turned upside down
a hog is a greedy person

annotation.surface: A man once upset greedy people and prickly types alike.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Prickly sorts' sounds like touchy people but means spiny animals.
annotation.definitionFit: Hedgehogs are covered in spines, so they are literally prickly creatures.

clue.text: Power boat in recreational area (4)

blocks.note: an ark is a boat, like Noah's

annotation.surface: A powerboat sits in a leisure area, perhaps on a boating lake.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Power boat' reads as one thing, a powerboat, but splits into two pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A park is an open area set aside for recreation.

clue.text: A guy touring Morecambe with bagel and coffee (9)

indicators.note: the guy travels around Morecambe, enclosing him

blocks.note: a bagel is ring-shaped, like the letter O

annotation.surface: A man takes the comedian Morecambe on tour, with a bagel and a coffee for the road.
annotation.walkthrough: Eric Morecambe was half of Morecambe and Wise, a much-loved British comedy double act; Morecambe is also a seaside town, which is what 'touring' suggests. A + M(ERIC)AN + O.
annotation.definitionFit: An americano is espresso diluted with hot water.

clue.text: Oscar and Margaret with a character from Greece (5)

blocks.note: Oscar is O in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Two friends, Oscar and Margaret, are joined by a Greek person.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Character' looks like a person in a story; it is a letter of the Greek alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Where I’d see a fun novel – Goodbye to Berlin? (3,11)

indicators.note: the letters are made new, i.e. rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone muses on where a fun book might be found, naming Isherwood's novel Goodbye to Berlin.
annotation.walkthrough: Goodbye to Berlin is a real novel by Christopher Isherwood, so 'novel' looks like a description of it. The question mark marks the definition as a playful one: goodbye as said in Berlin.
annotation.definitionFit: Auf Wiedersehen is German for goodbye, the farewell a Berliner would say.

clue.text: Pleasingly made light, full, yummy sandwiches (12)

indicators.note: the words hold the answer between them like a sandwich filling

annotation.surface: A food review praises sandwiches that are light, filling and tasty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' looks like the food in the review but works as a verb: the phrase holds the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Delightfully and pleasingly are both adverbs meaning in an agreeable way.

clue.text: Queen behind special, posh hotel getting mixture of wine and water (8)

blocks.note: the Ritz, a famously grand London hotel
ER = Elizabeth Regina; 'behind' puts it last

annotation.surface: The Queen sits at the back of a special gathering in a smart hotel, ordering a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Behind' tells you to place the Queen after the other pieces. The Ritz is a luxury hotel in London.
annotation.definitionFit: A spritzer is a drink of wine mixed with soda water.

clue.text: Criminal in the main is furious, pursuing power (6)

indicators.note: to pursue is to follow after, so power comes first

annotation.surface: A criminal, mostly, is angry and hungry for power.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In the main' looks like 'mostly' but means at sea: the main is an old word for the ocean, as in the Spanish Main.
annotation.definitionFit: A pirate is a criminal who operates on the open sea.

clue.text: What golfers produce with wedges of fried potatoes and spicy sauce initially (4,5)

indicators.note: take only the first letter of sauce

annotation.surface: A menu offers potato wedges with a spicy sauce.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain chips are thick fries. The pieces don't break where the answer's words do. Wedges are also golf clubs, the very ones golfers use for this stroke.
annotation.definitionFit: A chip shot is a short lofted golf stroke onto the green.

clue.text: Don, breaking weapon, produces expletive (5-4)

indicators.note: don splits the weapon open and sits inside it

blocks.note: a sword is a weapon; it goes around the next piece
to don is to put on, or wear

annotation.surface: A man called Don breaks a weapon and curses.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Don' is capitalised to look like a name but is the verb meaning put on clothes. S(WEAR)WORD.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an expletive is a rude oath.

clue.text: Nicest ode composed, divided into parts (9)

indicators.note: the letters are put together in a new arrangement

annotation.surface: A poet writes a lovely ode, arranged in stanzas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Composed' fits the poem so neatly that it hides its job of rearranging.
annotation.definitionFit: Sectioned means cut or divided into sections.

clue.text: A taxi reversing, one displaying old counters (5)

indicators.note: the taxi backs up, so its letters run backwards

blocks.note: a cab is a taxi; turned back

annotation.surface: A taxi backs up with its dashboard showing old meters.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Counters' suggests people or shop counters; here it means counting frames.
annotation.definitionFit: Abaci, the plural of abacus, are old bead frames used for counting.

clue.text: A fun activity on day hosting northern Greek king (9)

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sits on top of the next
the day holds the N inside it, as a host holds a guest

blocks.note: a game is a fun activity
MON = Monday; it wraps the next piece

annotation.surface: Someone plans some fun on a day when a Greek king from the north is visiting.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed after. He led the Greeks in the Trojan War, which makes 'hosting' him a grand visit.
annotation.definitionFit: Agamemnon was the legendary king of Mycenae in Greek myth.

clue.text: Old English person, one that’s possibly obtuse? (5)

blocks.note: one of the Germanic people who settled England and gave it its name
in geometry, obtuse means over 90 degrees

annotation.surface: An old-fashioned Englishman is suspected of being rather dim.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Obtuse' reads as slow-witted about the person, but it is the geometry term.
annotation.definitionFit: The Angles gave England its name; an angle can be acute, right or obtuse.

clue.text: Chap is too strange, a very cruel person (9)

indicators.note: the letters are made odd, i.e. rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone says a man is not just odd but downright cruel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Strange' reads as a description of the chap, sitting naturally beside 'too'.
annotation.definitionFit: A sociopath is a person with no conscience who may act with great cruelty.

clue.text: Product from overseas this person’s left on a boat (6)

blocks.note: this person is = I'm, the speaker
port is the left side of a ship

annotation.surface: A trader says a foreign product was left behind on a boat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like 'abandoned'; it is the direction, and on a boat that is port.
annotation.definitionFit: An import is goods brought in from another country.

clue.text: Small change for Trump’s former right-hand man (5)

blocks.note: the smallest British coins, hundredths of a pound
Mike, the vice president in Trump's first term

annotation.surface: A political jibe that Trump's old deputy was worth only small change.
annotation.walkthrough: Pence is the plural of penny, the British hundredth of a pound.
annotation.definitionFit: Pence are low-value coins; Mike Pence was Trump's vice president.

clue.text: Lane with five bats and foliage around grapes (4,4)

indicators.note: bats is slang for crazy, so the letters go mad

blocks.note: anagram fodder, joined to LANE by 'with'

annotation.surface: A lane is home to five bats among the leaves around a grapevine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Five' tempts you to use V, but the whole word is fodder. 'Bats' looks like the animals; it is slang for mad.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: grapes hang among the leaves of the plant they grow on.

clue.text: The setter caught plugging records, great works (5)

indicators.note: the pieces fill a gap inside the records, like a plug

blocks.note: EPs = extended-play records; they go around the next pieces
the setter refers to himself as I

annotation.surface: The setter promotes his records, calling them great works.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plugging' reads as promoting the records; it means filling them. EP(I C)S.
annotation.definitionFit: Epics are long, grand works such as heroic poems or films.

clue.text: Proclaim person at wild parties loses head (4)

indicators.note: the first letter is taken off

blocks.note: a raver goes to raves; minus R

annotation.surface: Someone declares that a partygoer has lost his head.
annotation.walkthrough: A rave is a wild dance party; 'head' is the first letter, not the partygoer's wits.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to declare something firmly.

clue.text: Unorthodox place to find nuns interrupting wedding with Albert (14)

indicators.note: the nuns' home breaks into the middle of the wedding
Albert is added after the rest

blocks.note: a wedding is a union; it goes around the next piece

annotation.surface: Nuns burst into a wedding, which is an unusual scene.
annotation.walkthrough: UN(CONVENT)ION + AL.
annotation.definitionFit: Unconventional and unorthodox both mean not following accepted ways.

clue.text: Money senior journalist is offered (8)

annotation.surface: An editor is offered cash.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Money' is the legal-tender sense of the word, not the adjective meaning gentle.
annotation.definitionFit: To tender is to offer formally, so tendered means offered.

clue.text: On the radio, Cher’s partner is cheerful (5)

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard, not seen, so the sound counts

blocks.note: Sonny Bono, Cher's partner in the duo Sonny and Cher

annotation.surface: A radio presenter says Cher's partner is in a good mood.
annotation.walkthrough: Sonny and Cher were a 1960s-70s American singing duo, famous for 'I Got You Babe'.
annotation.definitionFit: Sunny describes a bright, cheerful disposition.
